name: graph rotation system

data.structure: a graph rotation system assigns a cyclic ordering of edge-ends at each vertex
data.consequence: uniquely determines a graph embedding on an orientable or non-orientable surface, hence the surface
data.attribution: Edmonds 1960, developed in Gross and Tucker 1987

quote: a graph rotation system uniquely determines a graph embedding on an orientable or non-orientable surface, and thus uniquely determines the surface

name: edge twisting / extended graph rotation system

data.typing: an edge has type 0 if untwisted, type 1 if twisted
data.mechanism: edge is a flat paper strip; twisting one end 180 degrees clockwise changes the face boundary walks in the rotation system
data.effect: induces a new link projected on the surface

quote: An important concept in graph rotation systems is edge twisting. An edge has type 0 if it is untwisted and type 1 if it is twisted

name: cyclic plain-weaving (formal definition)

data.carrier: link L projected onto orientable surface S
data.condition1: no triple intersections at a single point on S
data.condition2: traversal of each component alternates over and under at every crossing

quote: a cyclic plain-weaving on an orientable surface S is a projection of a link L on S, such that (1) there are no triple intersections at a single point

name: over/under alternation guarantee (Theorem 2.1)

data.hypothesis: rho_0(G) untwisted rotation system embedding G on orientable surface S_h; A an arbitrary subset of edges
data.conclusion: twisting all edges in A yields a rotation system inducing a cyclic plain-weaving on S_h
data.proof_location: deferred to companion technical report Akleman et al. 2009

quote: If we twist all edges in A, then the resulting graph rotation system induces a cyclic plain-weaving on Sh

name: Face-Tracing Algorithm

data.purpose: extract the boundary-walk cycles (the link) from a graph rotation system
data.step2: update trace type t = t0 + type(edge) mod 2
data.step4: loop tracing and advancing until returning to start edge and type
data.outer_loop: Trace-All-Faces calls FaceTrace on every untraced face corner in rho(G)
data.result: collection of graph cycles that are the boundary-walks of the faces, i.e. a link projected on S

quote: A fundamental algorithm on graph rotation systems, known as face-tracing, is given immediately above. This algorithm applied to a graph rotation system ρ(G) on a surface S returns a collection of graph cycles that are the boundary-walks of the faces

name: projection method (PR) for twisted-edge weaving

data.precondition: all edges of the mesh are twisted
data.step1: Construct PR Control Polygons: trace face walks; displace each half-edge to p_i,j = (p1+p2)/2 + (-1)^j h e_i n_i; substitute into walk
data.step2: Construct PR Control Ribbons: assign a plane per half-edge; build non-planar edge-region quad (2 endpoints + 2 face centers); project onto both planes; take bilinear fractional sub-quad via parameters c,w; connect two pieces with quadrilateral connectors in face-trace order
data.step3: Construct PR Control Yarn: define an ellipsoid per internal edge; sample into n-sided convex polygon; connect polygons into a generalized toroid
data.step4: Construct Smooth Ribbons/Yarns: cubic Bezier smoothing of control ribbons (G1 continuous); offline Catmull-Clark subdivision of control yarns
data.gap_control: dense weaving at c~1, w~1, small h; sparse weaving at small c,w; gap closing improves as dihedral angle theta between adjacent faces approaches 180 degrees

quote: The algorithm of the projection method consists of four main steps. The first step is to construct a control polygon which we call the PR control polygon

name: gap valence / Schlafli-like weaving notation

data.gap: each quadrilateral ribbon piece is surrounded by four gaps corresponding to the edge's two endpoints and two adjacent faces
data.gap_valence: number of ribbons around a gap
data.notation: four-tuple (d0,d1,d2,d3) giving the two endpoint valences and two adjacent-face side counts

quote: The number of ribbons around a gap defines the shape of the gap. We call this the valence of the gap

name: Figure 3: twisting an edge of a mesh

data.panels: an untwisted edge vs. a twisted edge, shown as a paper strip
data.role: canonical illustration of the edge-twist operation underlying the whole theory

quote: Figure 3: Twisting an edge of a mesh on a surface S.

name: Figure 5: steps of the projection method on a twisted cube

data.panels_a_to_i: initial cube with all edges twisted; projection planes; edge-region quads; one projected region; all projected edge-regions; planar piece pairs; pink connector quads; colored control mesh (one color per cycle); final smooth ribbon

quote: The steps of the projection method (PR). (a) The initial mesh, a cube, with all its edges twisted, to create a cyclic plain-weaving

data.models: Venus (5 cycles), bunny (8 cycles), rocker arm (2 cycles), genus-3 object (16 cycles)
data.rendering: constructed with extruded ribbons on the mesh surface

quote: Venus consists of five distinct cycles. The bunny has eight cycles, the rocker arm has only two cycles, and the genus-three object has 16 cycles

name: Hamiltonian cycle

data.path_def: a Hamiltonian path visits each vertex of an undirected graph exactly once
data.cycle_def: a Hamiltonian cycle is a Hamiltonian path that closes into a cycle
data.existence: not every graph has a Hamiltonian cycle

quote: A Hamiltonian cycle (or Hamiltonian circuit) is a Hamiltonian path that is a cycle. Note that not every graph has a Hamiltonian cycle

name: single covering curve construction

data.core_rule: connect the centers of every two neighboring triangles in the Hamiltonian triangle strip
data.property: curve follows the mesh surface, meandering like a river
data.smoothing: the resulting control polygon is turned into a smooth curve with a parametric curve such as B-Spline

quote: These curves are constructed by connecting the centers of every two neighboring triangles in the Hamiltonian triangle strips

name: Hamiltonian triangle strip existence (Taubin)

data.claim: any quadrilateral manifold mesh without boundary can be re-triangulated so its dual has a Hamiltonian cycle
data.algorithm: split each quad along a diagonal, then flip edges until triangles form one strip

quote: every connected manifold quadrilateral mesh without boundary can be represented as a single Hamiltonian generalized triangle strip cycle

name: surface covering curve construction (6 steps)

data.step1: Initial Mesh: any manifold mesh, convex faces preferred
data.step2: Quadrangulation: apply a quad-conversion subdivision (dual of Simplest) if not already quad
data.step3: Initial Triangulation: insert a red diagonal into every quad, giving each triangle two black edges and one red edge
data.step4: Control Vertex Position Computation: weighted average per triangle p_cv = (2p0,0+p1,0+p1,1)/4, favoring the shared vertex
data.step5: Initial Curves: connect control points across shared black edges, one closed curve per original face
data.step6: Combining Curves: flip red diagonals lying between two separate curves to merge them, until one curve remains

quote: Our approach can be considered a 2-step process: (1) identify an Hamiltonian cycle that connects vertices of the dual of a given mesh

name: duotone surface

data.basis: vertex-insertion schemes like Catmull-Clark subdivision leave the quadrilateral mesh vertices always two-colorable
data.result: a single surface covering curve serves as boundary separating the surface into two paintable regions
data.implementation: Truchet-tile textures per quadrilateral, consistent with diagonal colors

quote: it is always possible to create a single curve that covers the whole surface such that all vertices in the first group are on one side

name: Jordan curve theorem and genus limitation

data.planar_case: any simple closed curve in the plane separates it into an inside and an outside region
data.surface_case: only correct for genus-0 surfaces; a positive-genus surface curve need not separate it

quote: Jordan's theorem is only correct for genus-0 surfaces. Any single curve on a surface with positive genus does not necessarily separate the surface

name: Theorem 1: bipartite Yellow/Blue graph connectivity

data.setup: U0,U1 edge-disjoint vertex sets of a bipartite graph; Y,B the Yellow and Blue graphs
data.claim: it is always possible to make Y and B each connected

quote: For a bipartite graph, say U0 and U1 are the two edge disjoint vertex sets and Y, B are Yellow and Blue graphs respectively. Then, we can make Y and B connected

name: Lemma 1: genus-0 tree/tree duality

data.claim: if one of the Yellow/Blue graphs is a spanning tree, the other is necessarily also a spanning tree

quote: If one of the Y/B graphs is a tree, then the other is also a tree.

name: duotone-surface algorithm

data.step1: convert input mesh to a 2-colorable quad mesh via Catmull-Clark or dual-of-Simplest subdivision
data.step2: 2-color vertices Blue/Yellow so no edge joins same-colored vertices
data.step3: triangulate each quad along a same-colored diagonal, choosing between two Truchet-tile textures
data.step4: flip diagonals between two separate same-color curve components, swapping that diagonal's color, until
data.step5: one closed curve remains, pure-yellow on one side and pure-blue on the other

quote: Choose a diagonal edge and flip it if it is between two separate curves. After the flip, reconstruct the curve.

name: Figure 6: Hamiltonian cycle construction and curve generation walkthrough

data.panels: initial mesh; dual-of-Simplest quadrangulation; red-diagonal triangulation; curve control vertices; per-face curve loops; all loops; a selected diagonal; flipped diagonal with recomputed vertices; merged curve; final single curve

quote: Visual presentation of the Hamiltonian cycle construction and curve generation algorithm

data.fig15: Catmull-Clark vertex insertion producing a 2-colored quad mesh (vertex-vertices vs edge-vertices)
data.fig16: the two possible diagonal triangulations of one quadrilateral
data.fig17: the paired Truchet-tile textures assigned to each triangulation choice

quote: Conversion of a given mesh into a 2-colorable quadrilateral mesh by using Catmull-Clark subdivision

name: piecewise linear mesh

data.condition: every edge is a straight line segment and every face is planar
data.generalization: includes non-triangular faces of varying valence, not only triangular meshes

quote: We say that a mesh M is piecewise linear if every edge of M is a straight line segment, and every face of M is planar

name: Gauss-Bonnet theorem (smooth statement)

data.statement: the integral of Gaussian curvature over a closed smooth surface equals 2 pi times the Euler characteristic
data.limitation: requires a smooth surface; motivates the discrete version proved in this paper

quote: the integral of the Gaussian curvature over a closed smooth surface is equal to 2π× the Euler characteristic of the surface which is 2 − 2g

name: Euler equation and Lemma 2.1 (v,e,f from average valence and genus)

data.lemma_2_1: expresses e, v, f of any piecewise linear mesh in terms of average vertex valence m-bar, average face valence n-bar, and genus g
data.proof_basis: each edge counted twice in vertex valences and twice in face boundaries, so sum(m_i) = sum(n_j) = 2e

equations: e = n_bar m_bar (2 - 2g) / (2 n_bar + 2 m_bar - n_bar m_bar)
v = 2 n_bar (2 - 2g) / (2 n_bar + 2 m_bar - n_bar m_bar)
f = 2 m_bar (2 - 2g) / (2 n_bar + 2 m_bar - n_bar m_bar)
quote: Let M be a piecewise linear mesh. Suppose that M has v vertices, e edges, f faces, and genus g. Let m and n be the average vertex valence and average face valence

name: angle deflection at a vertex

data.formula_role: discrete angle-deficit at a single vertex, generalizing angle deficit to non-regular meshes

quote: The angle deflection at vertex µi is defined as θ̄(µi) = 2π − ∑ θ j where θ j is the internal angle of the j-th corner

name: Calladine discrete Gaussian curvature

data.role: prior discrete Gaussian curvature definition, cited and distinguished from the paper's own SAD quantity
data.distinction: unlike SAD, the sum of Calladine curvature over a mesh need not equal 2 pi (2-2g)

equations: Gaussian curvature = Angular Deflection / Area Associated with Vertex
quote: the most popular discrete version of Gaussian curvature introduced by Calladine for triangular meshes uses angular deflection

name: Sum of Angle Deflections (SAD)

data.formula_role: mesh-wide sum of the per-vertex angle deflection
data.invariance: closely related to mesh geometric shape but proved to be a topological invariant in Theorem 2.2

quote: The sum of angle deflections (SAD) of the mesh M is defined as θ̄(M) = ∑ θ̄(µi)

name: discrete Gauss-Bonnet theorem (Theorem 2.2)

data.claim: the SAD of any piecewise linear mesh of genus g equals 2 pi (2 - 2g)
data.proof_route: sum interior face angles (n_j - 2) pi per face; sum 2 pi - theta_bar(mu_i) per vertex; combine via Euler equation
data.consequence: SAD is independent of vertex/edge/face counts and average valences, depends only on genus

quote: Let M be a piecewise linear mesh of genus g. Then the SAD θ̄(M) of the mesh M is equal to 2π(2 − 2g)

name: fixed-genus subdivision valence limit

data.derivation: from Euler equation and Lemma 2.1 in the limit of arbitrarily many faces at fixed genus
data.consequence: average face valence cannot exceed 6 without introducing valence-2 vertices or bigons; explains why (3,6), (4,4), (6,3) regions dominate common subdivision schemes

quote: This result says that the average face valence cannot exceed 6 regardless of what we do

name: branch construction via paired critical points

data.principle: since SAD is a fixed topological invariant, any local angle-deflection gain must be balanced by an equal loss elsewhere
data.extrusion_step: extruding a 4-valent quad face yields 4 vertices at valence 5 and 4 vertices at valence 3 (net-zero average change)
data.wrinkle_step: wrinkle operation yields 4 vertices at valence 4, 2 at valence 3, 2 at valence 5
data.quad_modeling_rule: minima/maxima require 3-valent vertices; saddles require valence greater than 4

quote: if we gain angle deflections in some vertices, we will lose some angle deflections in some other vertices

name: Figure 3: Morse-theory critical point sum

data.sequence: genus-0, genus-0, genus-1, genus-1, genus-2 object sequence
data.marking: +1 at each minima/maxima (convex/concave) critical point, -1 at each saddle point
data.claim: the marked total equals 2 - 2g in every case

quote: The total adds up to (2−2g) if we assign minima/maxima points +1 and saddles −1

name: rotation at a vertex

data.definition: a cyclic ordering of the set of edge-ends incident at that vertex
data.theorem_cited: a rotation system specifies a graph embedding and every graph embedding can be specified by a rotation system (Theorem 3.2.2 of Gross and Tucker 1987)

quote: A rotation at a vertex of a graph is a cyclic ordering of the set of the edge-ends that are incident at that vertex

name: extended graph rotation system (EGRS) with signed helical twists

data.model: each edge is a paper strip that can be twisted clockwise or counter-clockwise in a helical sense
data.twisted_strands: both strands cross over the edge and over each other
data.states: exactly two twisted states, +1 (counter-clockwise) and -1 (clockwise), plus the 0 (untwisted) state

quote: In extended graph rotation systems, an edge is viewed as a paper strip that can be twisted clockwise or counter-clockwise in helical sense

name: single-cycle twist condition (Theorem 2.1)

data.setup: rho(G) obtained from a mesh by possibly twisting some edges, inducing a weaving with at least two distinct cycles
data.operation: if edge e's two sides belong to two different cycles c1,c2, twisting e merges c1 and c2 into one cycle
data.consequence: repeated application always reduces the number of cycles to exactly one
data.mechanism: twisting an edge at the intersection of two faces merges those two faces into one face; cycles are face boundaries

quote: If we twist e, then we combine the two cycles c1 and c2 into one cycle and reduce the number of cycles in the weaving by one

name: single-cycle weaving via dual spanning tree

data.step1: build the dual mesh M* of the original mesh M
data.step2: compute any spanning tree T of M*
data.step3: twist every primal edge of M whose dual edge lies in T
data.step4: this merges all faces of M into one face, i.e. one cycle, using the minimum possible number of twists (|T| = F-1 edges)

quote: if we construct a spanning tree T in the dual mesh M, then twisting all the primal edges in M would merge all the faces in the original mesh M into a single face

name: minimum twisted-edge count and spanning-tree counting

data.mu_bound: average face valence mu is at least 3 and at most a little more than 6 for large polyhedral meshes of any genus
data.twist_range: minimum twisted edges lies between 0.33E and 0.66E depending on mesh type
data.cayley: for a complete dual graph, the number of spanning trees follows Cayley's formula
data.recursion: deletion-contraction recursion for the number of spanning trees of a general graph
data.probability_result: with probability 1 a random graph has 2^(F-1) single-cycle embeddings

quote: with probability 1, there are 2^{F−1} single cycle embeddings of G

name: extended projection method for untwisted edges

data.step1: project the initial mesh to a local plane
data.step2: connect each face center to its vertices, forming a radial-graph edge-region quadrilateral per edge
data.step3a: for twisted edges, project the edge-region to two small planar regions slightly above and below the plane
data.step3b: for untwisted edges, instead create two side-by-side quadrilaterals within the original plane
data.step4: form strips via bilinear interpolation with width w and length/steepness c; twisted edges yield a crossing '×' shape, untwisted edges yield two parallel non-crossing strips
data.step5: connect strips into a control-strip ring; smooth via B-Spline/Bezier for ribbons or convert to toroidal control yarn and subdivide for yarns

quote: For every twisted edge, project the corresponding edge-region to two small planar regions, one slightly above and the other slightly below the original plane

name: Figure 3: canonical edge twist-state legend

data.panel_a: plain undirected edge drawing, not considered twisted

quote: twisted edges can only be in one of two possible states. These states are shown in (c) +1 (i.e. counter-clockwise) twisted or (d) −1

name: Figure 4: octahedron before/after twisting demonstrating Theorem 2.1

data.before: an octahedron with all-untwisted edges has 8 unlinked face-boundary-walk cycles in 3D
data.after: twisting some edges links the cycles together into fewer, crossing cycles

quote: the eight face-boundary walks of the octahedron are unlinked in 3D. However, if some edges are twisted as shown in (d), then the cycles represented by the boundary walks become linked, as in (f)

name: single-cycle color convention

data.uniform_color_use: proves single-cycle-ness visually since only one color is theoretically needed for one thread
data.rainbow_color_use: hue changes continuously along the cycle to make the winding, self-crossing path legible

quote: For single-cycle woven objects, we changed the hue of the ribbon color (rainbow coloring) along the cycle to show the structure
